Meeting header:

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Quick partner intro. TerraMatrix is evaluating a hybrid GPU connector to resell GPU capacity and integrate onboarding with Redwood's runtime. TRANSCRIPT:
[00:00:02] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining — um this is Alex from Redwood, AE. we have Priya and Jon on the line too. how's everybody doing?
[00:00:12] Sam Ortega: hey Alex, good morning from our side. excited to chat.
[00:00:17] Maya Lin: morning, yea thanks for setting this up. we have Ravi and Ellen as well.
[00:00:21] Alex Chen: awesome. quick round robin — why don't we go through TerraMatrix's goals and then we can share how Redwood typically patterns hybrid GPU connectors.
[00:00:30] Sam Ortega: sure. high level: TerraMatrix runs a channel + reseller program, we want to offer managed GPU bursts to enterprise customers but keep control of billing and security. looking for a partner to provide a "connector" stack — basically an on-prem or edge agent that routes inference requests into our orchestration and to Redwood when customers want hosted inference.
[00:00:48] Ravi Patel: yeah and importantly we need predictable latency for some customer SLAs — that means we need to understand batch sizing, kv cache warmup behavior, and fallback policies.
[00:00:58] Priya Nair: when you say connector, do you mean agent on the customer's side or on TerraMatrix-managed edge?
[00:01:05] Sam Ortega: terra matrix managed edge locations. we operate a fleet of 40 edge racks in EMEA and NA. we want to route either to local GPU or Redwood hosted depending on capacity, cost, and SLA.
[00:01:18] Jon Ramos: got it. in our typical pattern we provide a lightweight control plane client that you can deploy in your VPC or on an edge host. it handles secure tunnels, token exchange, and can be configured to prefer local pools then fallback to host. some customers call that onramp or gateway.
[00:01:34] Maya Lin: ok. can you explain more about the secure tunnels? our security team will want details on key management and audit logs.
[00:01:40] Priya Nair: sure — we support multiple modes. for Redwood Dedicated or Private we can do customer managed V P C peering or mTLS tunnels. key material can be stored in your KMS; we support AWS KMS and HSM integrations. audit logs and request traces are available through the Console and can be forwarded to your SIEM.
[00:02:00] Ellen Zhou: when you say 'forwarded' is that push or pull? we prefer pushing to our S3 bucket and also a Splunk endpoint.
[00:02:06] Alex Chen: both. we can push export logs to S3 or stream events to your logging endpoint. some partners use the push model to their own lake to avoid pulling credentials.
[00:02:15] Ravi Patel: latency question: if a request misses local cache and we cold start a quantized model, what's the typical tail latency? we have customers that need <200ms 95th for short prompts.
[00:02:26] Priya Nair: that depends on model size and quantization. for smaller 7B-class quantized models on A100/RTX-class equivalents we've seen 80–150ms for short prompts with optimized kernels. but if you have a large 70B model, warmup and kv fetch could push that up. also network hop to Redwood hosted adds 30–80ms depending on region.
[00:02:46] Sam Ortega: so we'd probably want to route critical low-latency traffic to the racks that have smaller models or local cache. can Redwood handle model variants automatically?
[00:02:55] Jon Ramos: yes, smart routing is part of the platform — policies can route by latency, cost, or model-quality label. you can define a policy that prefers local small-quant models for latency-bound customers and falls back to larger models for accuracy when latency budget allows.
[00:03:08] Maya Lin: one of our concerns is model format/quant — we use an internal quant pipeline that produces INT4 artifacts. will Redwood's runtime accept those or do we need to re-quantize?
[00:03:18] Priya Nair: we generally accept standard quant formats, but there are vendor-specific kernel paths. sometimes we need a small conversion or a compatibility layer. we'll want a sample artifact to test.
[00:03:27] Alex Chen: and part of the pilot we usually run a quick compatibility check — drop in a model artifact and run a smoke bench.
[00:03:33] Ravi Patel: ok good. on the business side — how does billing work if traffic goes through TerraMatrix edge but runs on Redwood hosted? who invoices who?
[00:03:42] Alex Chen: flexible. there are two common patterns: reseller model where TerraMatrix bills their customer and pays Redwood monthly (reconciled), or direct-pass where Redwood bills the end-customer and revenue-share is handled through partner agreements. we'll surface pricing and a partner contract template.
[00:03:58] Sam Ortega: the reseller route is preferred by our sales team; they'd like to keep the customer relationship.
[00:04:04] Alex Chen: noted. we'll flag that in partner terms.
[00:04:08] [00:04:08] maya: (inaudible) — excuse me, sorry i think my mic cut.
[00:04:12] Priya Nair: no worries. switching back — let's talk about deployment modes. TerraMatrix has edge racks and wants to optionally host a subset of models locally. how do you imagine model onboarding?
[00:04:23] Sam Ortega: ideally via CI/CD: we push model bundles to our internal registry and then control-plane instructs connector to pull. need signed artifacts and validation.
[00:04:33] Jon Ramos: that's our recommended pattern — signed model bundles with manifest including model hash, quant meta, and a small validation hook. the connector verifies signature, downloads, and performs a smoke inference to validate.
[00:04:44] Ellen Zhou: audit requirement — we need immutable logs of model hashes, who triggered deploy, and KMS reference. can you produce that?
[00:04:50] Priya Nair: yep, we can record model deployment events, hashes, and user identity information to the audit trail. we also support SSO (SAML) and RBAC so actions are mapped to users.
[00:04:59] Ravi Patel: network topology: are we doing NAT through your control plane or direct peer? our infra team worries about egress and maintaining compliance in EMEA.
[00:05:07] Alex Chen: either. many partners prefer direct V P C peering in EMEA to avoid egress. for edge racks we usually do an encrypted outbound tunnel to a regional endpoint. we can provide diagrams.
[00:05:17] Sam Ortega: perfect, please include both options.
[00:05:21] [00:05:21] speaker 6: (overlap)
[00:05:23] Priya Nair: i'd like to surface a technical constraint — continuous batching and KV cache behavior. if you have high variance in sequence length, batching windows can cause tail latency spikes. for low-latency SLAs you might want to use smaller batch thresholds or dedicate a fast path GPU pool.
[00:05:38] Maya Lin: that matches our concerns. we can earmark a few racks as "low-latency" with smaller batch sizes. how does Redwood suggest autoscaling for those?
[00:05:47] Jon Ramos: autoscaling can be policy-driven — scale on request concurrency or queue latency. we also offer a reserved capacity model if you want guaranteed throughput for key customers.
[00:05:57] Sam Ortega: cost question — what's the unit economics? our CFO will want a sample TCO for running a 40 rack fleet vs using Redwood hosted for bursts.
[00:06:06] Alex Chen: we can pull a modeled cost spreadsheet. typically hosted per-token cost is lower for large scale due to pooling, but when you include egress and rack ops the breakeven moves. we'll send a model transformer sheet that you can populate.
[00:06:18] Ravi Patel: security checklist: SOC2, ISO27001, penetration test reports, and data residency docs — we need to hand these to procurement.
[00:06:25] Priya Nair: yes, we'll share SOC2 Type II and current pen test summary; for Private deployments we can offer contract language for on-prem and data residency.
[00:06:33] Ellen Zhou: also MFA and SSO integrations. can Redwood integrate with Okta for provisioning?
[00:06:38] Alex Chen: yes, SAML/Okta is supported and we have SCIM provisioning for users.
[00:06:42] Sam Ortega: great. one specific ask — our customers sometimes want to run benchmarks against their own prompts. can we get a benchmark harness from Redwood?
[00:06:49] Priya Nair: we provide a benchmark harness and some scripts. we'll also provide guidance on how to run distributed latency tests and token accounting.
[00:06:57] Maya Lin: for the pilot scope, we'd like to do three things: 1) run compatibility on two model artifacts, 2) run a latency benchmark for low-latency customer scenario, 3) test the model deployment pipeline and audit logs.
[00:07:10] Alex Chen: sounds good. estimated timeline? how fast do you want to move?
[00:07:15] Sam Ortega: pilot in 4 weeks would be ideal. internal procurement review will take time but we'd like to show results to a top-customer in 6 weeks.
[00:07:23] Alex Chen: we can commit to scheduling the bench and compatibility run in that window.
[00:07:27] [00:07:27] priya: we'll need sample artifacts and network access to do a smoke test.
[00:07:31] Maya Lin: i'll open a secure share with artifacts after the call.
[00:07:34] Ravi Patel: and I'll add a list of target customer SLAs and sample prompts.
[00:07:38] Jon Ramos: one more technical note: kernel selection — if your edge racks are a mix of Nvidia and AMD hw we need to ensure the runtime picks the right op kernels. sometimes minor math differences show up in outputs. we'll test for functional parity as part of the bench.
[00:07:52] Sam Ortega: we do have AMD in some racks. good to call that out.
